Magnolia Grove Cemetery—Rootsweb:  Magnolia Grove Cemetery—Galveston.  THC Atlas:  “The Magnolia Grove Association, formed in 1870, made plans to establish a cemetery atop this ridge to serve the entire community of Galveston. The land chosen was divided into 25 sections. Association members purchased individual plots and on June 20, 1870, the cemetery was formally established. A storm that struck Galveston Island in 1875 severely damaged the cemetery grounds. The graveyard fell into disrepair soon after the storm. All cemetery property except previously purchased burial plots was repossessed in 1878. Shortly thereafter the association went bankrupt and the graves of members of as many as 22 families were removed to other graveyards. Nevertheless, burials continued in some sections of the cemetery for several years. By 1900 and after several land transactions, much of the original cemetery became the property of B. E. Mann and T. A. Cobb. Although the cemetery was again damaged in the storm of 1900, photographs reveal many gravestones here in 1922. In 1941 the city of Galveston exhumed the remaining marked gravesites as it began development of an airport. A section of the original cemetery was set aside as a permanent "green space" by the Galveston City Council in 1986. --Texas AtlasDirections: 2115 Terminal Dr., Galveston”NOTE:  endangered, unmarked burials may not have been moved

Maplewood Development is proposing construction of a business park on a 62-acre site in Sections 9-10, Township 30N, Range 23W (45.103039, -93.172274). The site is located near the intersection of County Road I and Fairview Avenue in the City of Arden Hills, Ramsey County, Minnesota.

The property, sometimes referred to as the 135 Primer Tracer Area, was formerly used by the United States Department of the Army as the Twin Cities Army Ammunition Plant (TCAAP) for the purpose of manufacturing component primers and tracing compounds, and testing ammunition for World War II, the Korean Conflict, and the Vietnam War. The property was improved with buildings, roads, and specialized infrastructure that was constructed in the 1940s and 1950s and is currently in various stages of disrepair. The decommissioning of TCAAP started in the late 1970s and plans to transfer and redevelop portions of the property have been ongoing since the 1980s. No current operations are located on the Project Site which is vacant.

The TCAAP facility once occupied 2,370 acres. The Project Site is part of 1,611 acres previously owned by the federal government with the Minnesota National Guard having a long-term lease over most of the land for the Arden Hills Army Training Site (AHATS). In 2023, the federal government held an auction administered by the General Services Administration (GSA) to sell the 62-acre Project Site "as is".

The entire TCAAP property is in the City of Arden Hills which comprises approximately the northern third of the city. The property is in the northwest quadrant of Arden Hills with access to US Highway 10, County Highway 9, and Interstate 35W. The Project Site is bounded by the National Guard Bureau's (NGB) AHATS on the north and east, Parcel A of the Rice Creek Regional Trail Corridor and NGB property on the south, and an access easement and Parcel B of Rice Creek Regional Trail Corridor on the west.

THC Atlas:  “Born the son of a ship captain in Rhode Island, Samuel Williams was apprenticed to his uncle in Baltimore after 1810 to learn business skills. After 1816 he lived in Buenos Aires, where he learned Spanish and its related culture. By 1819 he was working in New Orleans, where he might have met empresario Stephen F. Austin. Williams came to Austin's Texas colony in 1823, and became the empresario's translator and clerk. For his services and immigrant status, Williams received 11 leagues (48, 712 acres) of land. He married Sarah P. Scott in 1828; They had nine children. Williams and Thomas F. McKinney founded a mercantile firm in 1833 in Quintana at the mouth of the Brazos River. Williams had traveled to the United States in 1835 to sell bank stock when he learned of fighting in Texas. Using the partnership's credit, he made purchases for the Texas army. Williams and McKinney incurred expenses of $99,000 supporting the Texas revolution. By 1838 Williams was helping the Texas navy build seven ships. His firm had moved to Galveston, where the partners promoted development of the city with Michel Branamour Menard. Williams opened a bank in Galveston in 1848, and lived in this home until his death. He is buried in Galveston's Episcopal Cemetery. Rootsweb as Calvary Catholic, Galveston Island.  THC Atlas:  “Attracted by economic opportunities to be found here, a large number of Italian immigrants came to Galveston in the 19th century. In 1876, they formed the Italian Mutual Benevolent Society (Societa'Italiana di Mutuo Soccorso) to provide assistance to fellow immigrants. The society purchased a plot of land in Calvary Catholic Cemetery in 1888 and built this mausoleum, known as the Italian Vault. The structure exhibits Gothic style influences in its buttresses, gargoyles, and Corinthian columns flanking the entrance. The vault provides space for twelve crypts. It served as a permanent or temporary resting place for more than 70 deceased members until burial could take place in the cemetery. A number of Italian immigrants are interred in plots surrounding the mausoleum. Buried in this cemetery are Captain Clemente Nicolini, a member of the original vault building committee and a former Italian consulate who aided many immigrants; and Gioacchino Cassara, the first president of the Italian Benevolent Society. The vault also was used by members of the later organized Italian society, Stella d'Italia, and finally the the Sons of Italy. Froehling & Robertson, Inc.  (F&R) has completed a Limited Phase II Environmental Site Assessment (ESA) in general conformance with the scope and limitations of F&R Proposal Number 1462-267E of the Citgo gas station, convenience store, and carwash facility located at 1708 Williamson Road NW in Roanoke, Virginia.

This Limited Phase II ESA was performed in order to identify potential subsurface contamination associated with current and historic use of the property as a filling station.  The following is a summary of our findings and is not intended to replace more detailed information contained elsewhere in this report.  

The facility has been operated as a filling station since at least the early 1950s.  Several gasoline tanks are depicted on historic Sanborn Fire Insurance maps on the northwest corner of the property dating from 1951 to 1955.  The date of or method of closure (abandonment in place, removal, etc.) of the tanks is uncertain; however, based upon the Ground Penetrating Radar Survey (GPR) conducted on the site, it appears that tanks are not present in that corner.  

The facility currently operates four underground storage tanks (USTs) at the Property; three of the tanks contain gasoline and are located beneath the canopy among the dispensers.  Along the northern property margin is a remote fill area for this UST system comprising three fill ports and other access points surrounded by a relatively large concrete pad.  Based on information relayed by the site contact, this was initially believed to be a historic UST system; however, after a review of DEQ files that contain a site sketch depicting the system, it appears not to be the case.  The access points in this area have been filled with concrete at some historical point and are unusable.  

A fourth UST, located along the southern property margin contains kerosene; a separate dispenser is located adjacent to this UST.  

Other improvements at the site include a concrete slab and apparent drain along the western edge of the property, vacuums, bollards, etc.  This use of the concrete slab and drain improvement was not determined as part of this project.  

Based on the results of F&R?s sample collection and analysis, concentrations of petroleum hydrocarbons were identified at the facility as follows: 

?	Analytical results for Boring B-1 indicated concentrations of 61.0 mg/kg TPH-GRO and 550 mg/kg TPH-DRO at approximately 12 feet below the ground surface.  This boring was placed on the northwest corner of the property in the area presumed to have been improved by tanks from the early 1950s until an unknown time.  

?	Boring B-10 showed a TPH-GRO concentration of 0.95 mg/kg at approximately 12 feet below the ground surface.  This boring was placed to the west side of the unused remote fill port area.  

?	Boring B-11 showed a TPH-GRO concentration of 53 mg/kg and a TPH-DRO concentration of 140 mg/kg approximately 4 feet below the ground surface.  This boring was placed to the south side of the unused remote fill port area.  

?	Boring B-10 showed a TPH-GRO concentration of 0.85 mg/kg at approximately 12 feet below the ground surface.  This boring was placed to the east side of the unused remote fill port area.  

Laboratory results indicated that TPH-GRO and DRO concentrations within the remaining borings were below the detectable laboratory level.  

Based upon regulations stipulated in the Virginia Department of Environmental Quality (DEQ) Petroleum Program Technical Manual (Technical Manual), the laboratory analytical results should be reported to the DEQ per Articles 9 and 11 of the State Water Control law.
